procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 1.10.2012 of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi in Original Petition No.229 of 1997.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The complainant initially challenged an order of the NCDRC dated 21.05.2003 by filing Civil Appeal No. 8211 of 2003 in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal on 15.03.2011, observing that the NCDRC had decided the issue of delay in delivery of goods without appreciating the material and evidence on record. The matter was remitted back to the NCDRC for fresh consideration.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via two cross appeals (Civil Appeal No. 9106 of 2012) against the order passed by the NCDRC after the case was remitted back to them. The Supreme Court dismissed both appeals, declining to interfere with the NCDRC's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has committed any illegality or perversity in recording the ﬁ nding that there was delay in delivery of consignment.

facts: The consignment was booked on July 24, 1996.
The agent for the carrier provided a delivery schedule indicating the goods would arrive on July 29 and July 31, 1996.
When the goods did not arrive, a revised schedule was provided for delivery on August 6, 1996.
The consignment was ultimately delivered much later, between September 3 and September 12, 1996, approximately one and a half months after it was booked.
The carrier (respondent no. 1) never denied that the agent (respondent no. 2) acted on its behalf or that a delivery schedule had been promised.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the material and evidence on record.
It found that the significant time gap between the booking date (24.07.1996) and the actual delivery date (03.09.1996 to 12.09.1996) was an "admitted position" that clearly established a delay.
The Court noted that the carrier's agent had issued a time schedule for delivery, which contradicted any claim that there was no agreement for timely delivery.
The Court also pointed out that the carrier had never disowned its agent or the delivery promises made by the agent.
Based on these facts, the Court determined that the NCDRC's finding of a delay was based on evidence and was not illegal or perverse.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, concluding that the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) had not committed any illegality or perversity in its finding that there was a delay in the delivery of the consignment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the NCDRC was justiﬁ ed in not allowing the entire claim for compensation by calculating the total weight of the subject consignment in view of Rule 22 (2) of Schedule-III of the Carriage by Air Act, 1972 (as amended by the Hague Protocol).

facts: The appellant filed a complaint before the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) due to a delay in the delivery of a consignment.
In their complaint, the appellant specifically prayed for a sum of Rs. 20 lakhs as compensation for loss of business and reputation.

The appellant later argued that under Rule 22(2) of the Carriage by Air Act, 1972, the compensation should be calculated based on the total weight of the consignment (2507.5 Kg) multiplied by US $20 per Kg, which would result in an amount exceeding Rs. 20 lakhs.
The NCDRC awarded the appellant the Rs. 20 lakhs they had originally claimed, not the higher amount calculated under the Act.
law: The Supreme Court cited the legal principle ("trite law") that a party is not entitled to seek or be granted a relief which they have not specifically prayed for in their legal complaint or pleadings.
application: The Supreme Court examined the appellant's original complaint filed under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
It noted that the appellant had explicitly limited their claim for compensation for loss of business and reputation to Rs. 20 lakhs.
Although a higher amount might have been calculable under the Carriage by Air Act, the Court found that the appellant was bound by the amount they had requested in their own complaint.
Therefore, the NCDRC was correct in awarding only the Rs. 20 lakhs that was prayed for, as it could not grant a relief greater than what the appellant had sought.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument and upheld the NCDRC's decision. It reasoned that a party cannot be awarded more compensation than what they have specifically requested in their complaint. Since the appellant had only prayed for Rs. 20 lakhs, they were not entitled to a higher amount, even if such an amount could be calculated under the Carriage by Air Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has committed any illegality or perversity in recording the ﬁ nding that there was delay in delivery of consignment.
appellant_arguments: The shipments booked on 24.07.1996, which were supposed to be delivered by 31.07.1996, were delivered with a delay of more than 40 days.
The carrier's agent (respondent No. 2) had informed the complainant about a tentative date of arrival at the time of booking, establishing a time schedule for delivery.
The carrier (respondent No. 1) never disputed that respondent No. 2 was its agent or that a promise for delivery within 7 days was made.
respondent_arguments: There was no deficiency in service, and no specific instructions were given by the appellant regarding the delivery timeline, therefore time was not the essence of the contract.

The carrier should not be held liable for delay because the appellant knowingly sent the consignment via an airline with multiple stops (Kuwait, Chicago, Memphis), which would naturally take a long time.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the NCDRC was justiﬁ ed in not allowing the entire claim for compensation by calculating the total weight of the subject consignment in view of Rule 22 (2) of Schedule-III of the Carriage by Air Act, 1972 (as amended by the Hague Protocol).
appellant_arguments: The NCDRC was not justified in refusing the entire claim for compensation, which should have been calculated based on the total weight of the consignment.
respondent_arguments: The compensation awarded by the NCDRC is excessive, unjust, and unfair, and is based on conjectures and surmises.

cases.case_name: Dilawari Exporters v. Alitalia Cargo & Ors.
cases.principle: The onus to show that an act done by an agent was within the scope of his authority or ostensible authority is on the person claiming against the principal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The onus to prove that an agent's act was within the scope of their actual or ostensible authority lies with the person making a claim against the principal, and this can be demonstrated through practice or a written instrument.
obiter: An agent's authority may be express (given by words spoken or written) or implied (inferred from the circumstances of the case or the ordinary course of dealing).

A principal is bound by an agent's unauthorized acts or obligations if the principal's own words or conduct induced third persons to believe that such acts and obligations were within the scope of the agent's authority.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court upheld the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's (NCDRC) order on compensation because the appellant was bound by the amount sought in their original complaint. Despite arguing for a higher amount under the Carriage by Air Act, 1972, the appellant had only prayed for Rs. 20 lakhs in damages, and it is a settled legal principle that a party cannot be granted relief beyond what was specifically requested in their pleadings.
legal_tests_applied: It is a trite law that a party is not entitled to seek relief which he has not prayed for.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's claim for higher compensation was rejected because in its original complaint, the appellant had only sought damages for Rs. 20 lakhs as compensation for loss of business and reputation.
The court applied the established legal principle that a party cannot be granted relief that it has not specifically requested in its legal filings.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded because the court affirmed the NCDRC's decision, finding that the compensation awarded was appropriate in light of the appellant's own limited prayer for relief in the initial complaint.
